docs.title: detection-coverage-audit
docs.text:
A coverage heatmap counts rules. It cannot tell you whether a rule could ever fire on the telemetry you actually collect. This tool measures that difference.

Point it at a directory of Sigma rules and a parquet export of your telemetry. It reports, per rule, whether the log source exists, whether every field the rule keys on is populated, and how often. Then it rolls that up to ATT&CK technique level, because technique level is what a heatmap displays and technique level is where the illusion lives.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• How the audit works walks the pipeline from rule file to verdict.
  • Verdicts explains the five outcomes and what an engineer does about each.
  • The example report is generated on every docs deploy from the bundled rule pack and a freshly generated synthetic corpus.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install detection-coverage-audit

docs.title: The shortest useful run
docs.text:
dca generate-telemetry --events 200000 --out corpus.parquet --seed 7
dca audit --rules rules/ --telemetry corpus.parquet --out report.html

The first command exists so the tool can be evaluated without exporting anything from a production SIEM. Replace it with your own parquet export and the numbers stop being a simulation.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Four decisions shaped this tool more than any other, and each is written up with the options that were rejected and why:

  • ADR-001: measure field presence from a sample rather than replaying every event.
  • ADR-002: depend on a library rather than a cluster.
  • ADR-003: why the generator inserts through DataFrames.
  • ADR-004: why profiling is batched, and the out of memory error that forced it.

docs.title: How the audit works
docs.text:
The audit joins two things that are normally never compared: what the detection rules reference, and what the telemetry contains.

flowchart LR
  subgraph rules["Rule side"]
    A["Sigma rule files<br/>(.yml)"] --> B["loader<br/>tolerant parse"]
    B --> C["field extraction<br/>strip modifiers"]
    B --> D["ATT&CK tags<br/>attack.tNNNN.NNN"]
  end

  subgraph telemetry["Telemetry side"]
    E["parquet corpus<br/>(logsource_key, event)"] --> F["materialize sample<br/>reservoir, seeded"]
    F --> G["json_tree leaf expansion<br/>batched by rowid"]
    G --> H["field presence<br/>per log source"]
  end

  C --> I{{"join on<br/>logsource_key + field"}}
  H --> I
  I --> J["verdict per rule"]
  D --> K["technique rollup<br/>blind if every rule is blind"]
  J --> K
  K --> L["HTML report"]
  K --> M["JSON for CI"]
  K --> N["exit code<br/>for the gate"]

docs.title: The rule side
docs.text:
Rules are parsed tolerantly. A detection content repository in the real world always has a few files that do not parse, and an audit that aborts on the first one is an audit nobody runs. An unparseable file becomes a finding, because a rule that cannot be parsed is a coverage gap too.

Field extraction walks the detection block and takes every mapping key as a field name, stripping Sigma modifiers after the first pipe, so CommandLine|contains|all yields CommandLine. The condition key is not a field. A selection that is a flat list of scalars is a full text keyword search and names no field at all, which is tracked separately rather than counted as zero fields.

ATT&CK tags are read from the tags block. A sub-technique tag is attributed to its parent technique as well, because a coverage claim made at technique level is the claim a heatmap displays.

docs.title: The telemetry side
docs.text:
The corpus is a parquet file of (logsource_key, event) pairs where event is JSON. The profiler expands each event into its leaf fields and counts, per log source, how many events contain each field.

Two details here are load bearing.

Paths are reconstructed, not read off. DuckDB's json_tree reports the same fullkey of $.id.orig_h for a literal key containing a dot, which is how Zeek writes id.orig_h, and for a nested object, which is how CloudTrail writes userIdentity.type. The profiler builds each path from the parent path plus the leaf key and records which shape it saw, because the two need different field extractions in the SIEM and conflating them would make the report wrong in a way nobody could see.

Profiling is batched. Leaf expansion over a 10M event corpus produces roughly 65M rows, and deduplicating them in one statement exhausted DuckDB's memory budget during the build. Batches are contiguous rowid ranges, so no event is split and the per field tallies sum exactly. See ADR-004.

docs.title: The join
docs.text: For each rule: if its log source produced no events, the rule is blind and nothing else matters. Otherwise every referenced field is looked up in that source's measured presence. A field that never appears means the rule cannot fire. A field that appears below the configured threshold means the rule fires on a fraction of the events it was written for, which is a different problem with a different fix.

docs.title: The rollup
docs.text:
A technique is blind when every rule mapped to it is blind. One working rule is enough to cover a technique, which is the same standard a heatmap applies, so the comparison is fair.

That percentage is the headline number: the share of techniques your rule set claims to cover where nothing could actually fire.

docs.title: Verdicts
docs.text:
Five outcomes per rule. The ordering is deliberate: the audit reports the most severe thing that is true, so a rule whose log source is missing entirely is never reported as merely having a missing field.

Verdict Meaning Counts as blind What to do no_source The rule's log source produced no events in the corpus. yes Onboard the log source, or retire the rule. missing_field The source is present, but at least one referenced field never appears. yes Rewrite the rule against the field names this source emits, or extend the pipeline. unparseable The rule file could not be parsed. yes Fix or delete the rule file. rare_field Every field is present, but one falls below the presence threshold. no Confirm the field is populated often enough for the rule to be useful. keyword_only The rule full text searches the raw event and names no field. no Rewrite as a field based rule so coverage can be measured. resolved The source is present and every field is present above the threshold. no Nothing.

docs.title: Why missing_field is the common one
docs.text:
Most public detection content is written against Sysmon field names: Image, ParentImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess. An estate that audits process creation through Windows Security EventID 4688 instead populates NewProcessName and ParentProcessName. The rule is correct, the telemetry is present, the technique shows green on the heatmap, and the rule can never fire.

That single mismatch accounts for most of the blind techniques in the bundled example. It is the reason this tool exists.

docs.title: Condition branches
docs.text:
A rule's condition decides which of its selections have to match, and the audit resolves each alternative separately. This is real detection content, not a contrived case:

detection:
  selection_sysmon:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  selection_4688:
    NewProcessName|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  condition: selection_sysmon or selection_4688

On an estate collecting Windows Security EventID 4688 that rule fires through selection_4688. Resolving the union of every field would report it missing_field because Image is absent, which is wrong, and wrong in the direction that makes the tool look careless to the people who write rules well.

A rule is blind only when every branch its condition offers is blocked. The report shows the branch count and how many are blocked, so a rule that fires through one of two paths is visibly different from one that fires through both.

A negated selection is a filter. Its fields do not need to be present for the rule to fire, so they never make a rule look blind.

An aggregation tail after a pipe, | count() by host > 5, is ignored, because it changes when a rule fires rather than which fields it reads.

When a condition cannot be parsed, the audit falls back to requiring every selection, which is the old behaviour, and says so on the finding. A parse failure can therefore only make the audit more pessimistic, never more permissive. See ADR-005 for why this parser exists rather than pySigma's.

docs.title: Why rare_field is not blind
docs.text:
A field present in 0.04% of its source's events is not missing. A rule keyed on it will fire, occasionally, on the small share of events that carry it. Calling that blind would be wrong and calling it resolved would be worse, so it is its own verdict with its own action.

The threshold is configurable through DCA_RARE_FIELD_THRESHOLD and defaults to 0.001, meaning 0.1%. Note the interaction with sampling: a field rarer than roughly 1/N can be missed entirely by an N row sample and will then be reported as missing_field. See ADR-001 for why the error is allowed to point in that direction.

docs.title: Why keyword_only is separate
docs.text: A keyword rule searches the raw event text. There is no field to resolve, so field level coverage does not apply to it. Counting it as resolved would overstate coverage, counting it as missing would understate it. It gets its own category and its own action, which is to rewrite it so that its coverage becomes measurable at all.

docs.title: Gating CI on verdicts
docs.text:
dca gate exits 2 when the blind technique percentage exceeds a threshold or when there are more unparseable rules than allowed, which makes the audit a required check on a detection content repository rather than a report somebody remembers to read.

dca gate --rules rules/ --telemetry corpus.parquet \
  --max-blind-pct 40 --max-unparseable 0

Pick the starting threshold from the number the audit reports today, then ratchet it down. A gate set to a number the repository cannot currently meet gets disabled within a week.

docs.title: ADR-001: Measure field presence from a sample rather than replaying all telemetry
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-19

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The audit needs to know which fields a log source actually populates. There are three ways to find out.

Read the pipeline configuration. This is cheap and wrong: a field declared in a parser is not a field that arrives populated, and the gap between the two is exactly what this tool exists to find.

Replay the whole corpus. This is correct and expensive. Profiling measures

105,587 events per second on the hardware recorded in benchmark/results, so a 90 day window at 2,000 events per second, which is a small enterprise, is 15.5 billion events and roughly 41 hours of profiling. Nobody runs that weekly.

Sample the corpus. This is correct within a stated confidence bound and cheap.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Parse the pipeline configuration only. Rejected: it measures intent, not fact.
  2. Full replay, every run. Rejected on runtime for any realistic window.
  3. Full replay with incremental state across runs. Rejected for v1: it adds a state store and a cache invalidation problem to a tool whose first version should be a single command with no persistent state.
  4. Reservoir sample with a fixed seed, with full replay available. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Profile a reservoir sample of configurable size, seeded so a run is reproducible, and default to profiling everything so that a small corpus gets an exact answer with no flag. --sample N switches to sampling.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
A field that appears in fewer than roughly 1/N of events in its source can be missed by an N row sample, and the tool will report the rule that keys on it as blind when it is merely rare. That is the right direction for the error to point: a false blind finding costs an engineer five minutes of checking, a false coverage finding costs an undetected intrusion.

Sampling is reservoir rather than Bernoulli so the sample size is exact, and seeded so two runs over an unchanged corpus produce the same answer. Without the seed, a rare field would flicker in and out of the report between runs and nobody would trust it.

The RARE_FIELD verdict exists because of this decision. A field present in 0.04% of events is not missing and not usefully covered either, so collapsing it into either RESOLVED or MISSING_FIELD would have hidden a real finding.

docs.title: ADR-002: DuckDB over Elasticsearch for the telemetry side
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-19

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The audit has to scan a telemetry corpus and count field presence per log source. The obvious instinct in a security engineering team is to point the tool at the SIEM, because the data is already there. The less obvious question is what the tool should depend on in order to run.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Query the SIEM directly (Splunk REST, Elasticsearch _search). Attractive because the data is live. Rejected for v1: it makes the tool untestable without a cluster, couples it to one vendor's field naming, and means a developer cannot run it at all without production credentials. It also turns a weekly audit into load on the platform the SOC depends on.
  2. Stand up Elasticsearch locally for the corpus. Rejected: a container, a JVM heap to tune and an index mapping to maintain, in exchange for a full text engine whose strengths this workload never touches. The audit does aggregation over a columnar scan, which is the one thing Elasticsearch is worst at.
  3. Pandas in memory. Rejected on the 10M event scenario, where holding decoded JSON for the whole corpus is the dominant cost and the profile is already a single aggregation that never needs the whole corpus resident.
  4. DuckDB over parquet. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Read the corpus as parquet with DuckDB. The audit depends on a library, not a service. No container, no daemon, no credentials, no mapping.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The boring choice buys three things that matter more than novelty here.

The test suite runs with no external services, which is why make verify works on a clean checkout and in CI without a compose file. That is the single largest reason this repository can be cloned and verified in under two minutes.

json_tree gives recursive field extraction in SQL, which is the entire profiler. The alternative was walking decoded JSON in Python, which measured slower and would have been more code.

The cost is that the corpus has to be exported to parquet first rather than read live from the SIEM. For a weekly audit, an export is a scheduled job and this is not a real constraint. For an ad hoc "is this new rule going to fire" question, it is friction, and that is the trigger condition recorded in the Pivot section of the README for adding a Splunk ingestion path.

DuckDB's USING SAMPLE also made ADR-001's sampling a one line change rather than a sampling implementation.

docs.title: ADR-003: Insert generated events through chunked DataFrames
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-19

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The corpus generator writes synthetic events into DuckDB before copying them to parquet. The first implementation used executemany with a parameter list, which is the idiomatic DBAPI approach and is what most examples show.

Measured on the hardware recorded in benchmark/results:

Insert path Throughput 10M event corpus executemany, one row per bind 2,403 events/sec 69 minutes Chunked DataFrame registration 53,938 events/sec 3.1 minutes

The insert path alone measured 308 times faster in isolation; end to end the generator is 22 times faster, because JSON construction in Python then becomes the dominant cost.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. executemany. Rejected on the numbers above. A 69 minute generation step would have made the 10M event benchmark scenario impractical to run, which means it would not have been run, which means the scalability claim in the README would have been an extrapolation.
  2. DuckDB appender API. Comparable throughput, but it binds to a table created ahead of time and expresses the column types twice.
  3. Write parquet directly with pyarrow, bypassing DuckDB on the write path. Fastest in principle and rejected as a dependency the project otherwise does not need: DuckDB is already present for the read path.
  4. Chunked DataFrame registration. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Build rows in Python, then register each chunk of CHUNK_ROWS as a DataFrame and insert it with a single statement.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Peak memory is bounded by the chunk size rather than by corpus size, which is why the chunking is retained now that it is no longer needed for throughput. A 10M event corpus generates in about 3 minutes with a flat memory profile.

Output is byte identical to the executemany implementation at the same seed, verified with an EXCEPT over both parquet files, so the change carries no risk of having quietly altered the corpora that earlier numbers were measured on.

pandas becomes a hard dependency of the generator. It was already an indirect one through the test fixtures, and the alternative was adding pyarrow instead, so this costs nothing in practice.

docs.title: ADR-004: Profile the corpus in bounded batches
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-19

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The profiler expands each event into one row per leaf field with DuckDB's json_tree, deduplicates those rows per event, and counts them. The first implementation ran that as a single statement over the whole corpus.

At 100,000 and 1,000,000 events it worked and was fast. At 10,000,000 events it raised OutOfMemoryError: could not allocate block of size 256.0 KiB (4.6 GiB/4.6 GiB used).

The arithmetic is unsurprising in hindsight. Six to eight fields per event across 10M events is roughly 65M leaf rows, and the DISTINCT over (row id, log source, field, shape) has to hold a hash table proportional to that. Memory scaled with corpus size, which is the one thing a tool meant for 90 day windows cannot do.

This mattered beyond the error itself. The scenario that failed was the one the README's scalability claim depended on. Had the benchmark quietly skipped it, the published throughput figure would have been an extrapolation from 1M events presented as a measurement.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Raise memory_limit. Rejected. It moves the ceiling without removing it, and on a host with 8GB of RAM it trades a clean DuckDB error for the OS OOM killer, which is a much worse failure mode inside a scheduled job.
  2. SET preserve_insertion_order = false. DuckDB suggests this and it does reduce peak memory, but the saving is a fraction and the ceiling remains proportional to corpus size.
  3. Require sampling above some corpus size. Rejected as a silent accuracy change: the tool would have started answering a different question than the one asked, without the operator choosing that.
  4. Spill to disk via a persistent DuckDB database file. Workable, and rejected for v1 because it introduces a temporary file to manage, clean up and fail on when the disk is full.
  5. Aggregate over bounded batches of rows. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Materialize the sample once, then profile contiguous rowid ranges of BATCH_ROWS events each, summing the per field tallies in Python. Peak memory is set by the batch size, not the corpus size.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Correctness depends on one property: a batch is a contiguous rowid range, so no event is split across two batches, and therefore an event counted once for a field in its own batch is counted exactly once overall. Two tests assert this directly, including one that sweeps batch sizes of 1, 2, 7, 50, 100, 101 and 1000 over a 101 event corpus to catch an off by one at a boundary. Batched output was also verified identical to single statement output on a 1M event corpus.

The cost is a small amount of Python level aggregation per batch and the loss of one single statement elegance. In exchange, runtime stays linear and memory stays flat, which is what lets the 10M scenario be a measurement rather than a projection.

BATCH_ROWS is a module constant rather than a config value. It is a memory safety property of the implementation, not a knob an operator should be reasoning about, and the tests set it directly when they need to.

docs.title: ADR-005: Parse Sigma rules as YAML rather than with pySigma
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-19

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pySigma is the reference implementation of the Sigma rule format. It is well maintained, it is what the Sigma project itself uses, and reaching for it is the obvious default. This repository depended on it for several commits before anyone checked whether it was actually suitable, which is its own small lesson.

The audit has one requirement that turns out to conflict with how pySigma works. A rule file that cannot be parsed is a coverage finding, not an error. A detection content repository in the real world always contains a few files that are broken, half written, or committed as placeholders before their logic exists. An audit that aborts on the first one is an audit nobody runs twice, and worse, a broken rule file is itself a gap in coverage that the report should be telling someone about.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
pySigma 2.0.1, parsing three inputs:

Input Result A valid rule Parsed, one rule A rule with no detection block SigmaDetectionError: Sigma rule must have a detection definitions Malformed YAML ParserError from the underlying YAML parser

The decisive case was a multi document collection holding one valid rule and one rule with no detection block:

SigmaDetectionError: Sigma rule must have a detection definitions

One broken rule aborts the entire collection. The valid rule alongside it is never returned. On a pack of 500 rules, a single placeholder file would mean the audit reports nothing at all, and the operator would have no indication which file caused it beyond the exception.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. pySigma, abort on error. Rejected on the measurement above. It inverts the requirement: the tool would be least able to report on exactly the repositories that most need auditing.
  2. pySigma, one SigmaCollection per file, catching exceptions per file. Workable, and genuinely tempting. Rejected because it still cannot report per rule findings inside a multi document file, and because it makes pySigma's full validation strictness the definition of "parseable", which is stricter than this audit needs. A rule with an unusual status value or a tag pySigma does not recognise is still a rule whose field references can be read.
  3. pySigma for the valid subset, own parser for the rest. Rejected for v1 as two parsers for one format, which is a maintenance burden and a source of disagreement about what a rule means.
  4. Parse YAML directly and read the detection block. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Load rules with PyYAML, tolerate failure per document, and report unparseable files as UNPARSEABLE findings. Take field names from the detection block's mapping keys, stripping Sigma modifiers after the first pipe.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The loader is tolerant by construction: a YAML error, an absent detection block and a non mapping document each become a finding with a reason, and the audit continues. One test asserts this directly on a directory holding both a valid rule and a broken one.

The cost is real and worth stating plainly. This is not a Sigma implementation. It does not build an abstract syntax tree, resolve field mapping pipelines, apply backend conversion, or validate that a rule is well formed by the specification. It reads field references. For a coverage question that is sufficient, and for anything about rule semantics it is not.

Field extraction is one function, dca.rules.fields.extract_fields. If the audit ever needs real Sigma semantics, that function is the seam where pySigma comes back, applied to the valid subset of a pack, with the tolerant loader still in front of it to keep broken files reportable.

The dependency was removed rather than left declared and unused. An unused dependency in pyproject.toml is a claim the code does not support, and this one had already reached the README's tech stack table before it was caught.

docs.title: Forensics audit: detection-coverage-audit at v0.3.0
docs.text: Four personas, each auditing independently, then an integrated verdict. Graded PASS, WEAK or FAIL. Every FAIL found during this audit was fixed with its own commit before delivery, and the fix commits are named below.

docs.title: Persona 1: The Principal Engineer
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 Clone, run, verify PASS Tested literally, twice, in a clean directory from the README text alone. Failed the first time with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tests', fixed in fix(test): put the repo root on pythonpath so a fresh clone verifies, then re-tested: 100 tests pass in 8.4s with no network, no credentials and no containers. 2 Architecture and design decisions PASS Four packages with a real boundary each: rules reads detection content, telemetry measures what the corpus contains, audit joins them, report renders. The join is the only place the two halves meet, which is why adding an SPL parser touches one function. Five ADRs, each with rejected options. 3 Abstraction and configurability PASS Every tunable is on Config, sourced from the environment with validation that rejects out of range values. No module reads a literal path, threshold or field name. BATCH_ROWS is deliberately a module constant, not config, and the ADR says why. 4 Error handling and edge cases PASS Nine documented failure modes with detection, behaviour and recovery for each. Missing corpus, empty corpus, malformed schema and unparseable rule each have a distinct, tested path. The loader is tolerant by construction, which is a design decision with an ADR rather than an accident. 5 Testing PASS 100 tests, 99.2 percent branch coverage measured by pytest-cov, including regression tests for all nine bugs found during the build. The batch boundary test sweeps batch sizes 1, 2, 7, 50, 100, 101 and 1000 over a 101 event corpus.

docs.title: Persona 2: The UX Director and Product Thinker
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 First 30 seconds PASS Opens with the problem and a number, not with a technology. The bolded one-liner states what is found and the measured figure; the three bullets give pain, mechanism and result. 2 The So What of results PASS The blind technique percentage is tied to a consequence in plain words: "Every one of those rules parses, deploys, maps to a technique, turns the heatmap green, and can never fire. Nobody finds out until an incident review asks why nothing alerted." 3 Visual storytelling PASS after a fix Was WEAK. The performance chart plotted runtime against corpus size, which shows linear scaling that nobody disputes, while the surrounding prose claimed flat throughput. Replaced with a throughput bar chart in docs(readme): chart throughput rather than runtime under load. The architecture diagram labels the three boundaries where failures are handled; the HTML report leads with the headline number and themes for light and dark. 4 Actionability and handoff PASS Every finding in the report carries an action, and the mapping is a named table in code rather than prose. Future Work names the first metric to watch after deploying and says why the aggregate version of it would mislead.

docs.title: Persona 3: The Hiring Manager
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 Tutorial smell test PASS The problem is specific, current, and not in any tutorial: the gap between a coverage heatmap and the field names a log source actually populates. The Sysmon against EventID 4688 mismatch is a real failure mode in real estates. 2 Stolen Valor check PASS after a fix Was a FAIL. pysigma was declared in pyproject.toml and listed in the README tech stack table, and no module imported it: an advertised capability the code did not have. Removed in fix(deps): drop pysigma, which was advertised but never imported, after measuring what it would have done, with ADR-005 recording the measurement. The tech stack table now distinguishes what DuckDB provides, json_tree recursion, from what this project does with it, path reconstruction and shape detection. 3 Hardest problem solved PASS Two bugs that had been cancelling each other out since the first commit: a profiler that could not distinguish a literal dotted key from a nested path, and a generator that nested every dotted name. The writeup states plainly that a test would not have caught it, because the test would have shared the code's assumption. Both fix commits are linked. 4 One thing I will remember PASS That the tool found a bug in its own test data by being made more precise, and that the author said so in the README instead of quietly fixing it.

docs.title: Persona 4: The Sceptic (provenance)
docs.text:
Automated by scripts/provenance_check.py. Final run: 25 pass, 2 weak, 0 fail across 27 checks.

Three FAILs were found and fixed during this audit:

  1. tools/check_dashes.py held the forbidden characters as literals, so the one file whose job is to enforce the no-dash rule tripped its own check. Fixed in fix(tools): build the dash table from code points not literals.
  2. scripts/provenance_check.py repeated the same mistake with a second copy of the table. Fixed by deleting the copy and delegating, in fix(scripts): delegate the dash check instead of duplicating its table.
  3. The package description was 121 characters, one over the profile grid limit. Fixed in chore: trim the package description under the 120 character grid limit.

The two remaining WEAKs, both accepted with a reason:

  • 8 commit subjects exceed 72 characters. Left alone rather than rewritten. Rewriting history to tidy prose invalidates every clone and commit reference for no functional gain. tools/check_commit_subject.py now runs as a commit-msg hook so the count cannot grow.
  • 8 files still carry the identity placeholder. Expected: the repository was built before the GitHub account was known. tools/set_identity.sh binds every URL in one pass and has been tested twice in a scratch clone, including that it is idempotent and that it no longer rewrites its own search pattern.

docs.title: Integrated verdict
docs.text:
Overall portfolio score: 9 out of 10.

The repository holds up to all four reads. History is 52 commits of real work with no padding and no date manipulation, three annotated tags with a changelog that covers each one, badges that read endpoints CI writes rather than static claims, and 30 published numbers verified against measured values by a CI job. Nine bugs were found during the build, each with a regression test, and the two most interesting ones are written up rather than hidden.

It is a 9 and not a 10 because it has not been pushed yet: the Actions tab is not green because no run has happened, the releases are local tags rather than GitHub Releases, and the package is publish-ready rather than published. Those are the three things a sceptic checks that no amount of local work can satisfy.

docs.title: Critical failures (do not ship)
docs.text: None outstanding. All four FAILs found during this audit were fixed with their own commits, named above, and the affected checks re-run.

docs.title: Impact multipliers
docs.text:
The three changes that would take this from a 9 to a 10, in order:

  1. Push and publish. Green Actions tab, three GitHub Releases cut from the existing annotated tags, the docs site live on Pages so the badge endpoints resolve, and the package on PyPI through trusted publishing. This is the whole gap between 9 and 10 and none of it is more work than an afternoon.
  2. Run it against one real rule pack. Vendoring the public SigmaHQ Windows rules at a pinned commit and publishing the blind technique percentage against a real corpus would replace the single most questionable thing in the repository, which is that every number is a simulation. The simulation is honestly labelled, but a real number is worth more than an honest simulation.
  3. Ship field drift detection. Field presence per source is already computed every run and thrown away. Storing it would let the tool answer "which field did we silently stop collecting", which is the same class of failure arriving over time, and it is perhaps 200 lines on top of what exists.

docs.title: Elevator pitch
docs.text:
A coverage heatmap tells you a rule exists for a technique; it cannot tell you whether the field that rule keys on is in the telemetry you actually collect, and the gap between those two is where real intrusions go unnoticed. This tool joins Sigma rules to the field names measured in a telemetry export and reports which ATT&CK techniques are green on the heatmap and blind in production, with a CI gate so coverage regressions fail a pull request. On the bundled example,

63 percent of mapped techniques turn out to have no rule that could fire, mostly because public detection content is written for Sysmon field names and the estate collects Windows Security EventID 4688.

Note on the figure: this audit was run at v0.3.0, when the number was 66.7 percent. Condition aware resolution, merged after the audit, corrected one rule whose only missing field sat inside a filter clause, and the figure is now the value shown above. The pitch carries the tagged current number rather than the figure as it stood on the day.
